name: Amiloxate

lead: Amiloxate is a cinnamate-type UVB filter found in some sunscreens. People use sunscreens with filters like it to prevent sunburn and the cumulative photoaging that shows up as uneven tone and wrinkles.

It absorbs UVB radiation within the sunscreen film. Published work on it is mostly analytical and environmental, plus case reports of photoallergic contact dermatitis; its appearance benefit follows from the general effect of sunscreens.

paras: It is an ingredient in EU sunscreens, usually combined with other filters in a daily or holiday SPF. Benefits come from regular application over months and years rather than from a visible change after one use.
Photoallergic contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.

angle.text: Amiloxate is a cinnamate UVB filter found in EU sunscreens. By absorbing UVB it lowers sunburn, and over time less sun damage means skin stays more even and youthful. Published work on it consists mainly of analytical studies and photoallergy case reports.

lead: Amiloxate (isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate, isopentyl 4-methoxycinnamate, IMC) is a cinnamate ester used as a UVB filter in sunscreen products [1]. For appearance, sunscreen filters like it are used to limit UV exposure that causes sunburn, tanning, uneven pigmentation and visible photoaging, so skin keeps a smoother, more even look over time [2]. Amiloxate has been approved in the European Union since 1997; in the United States it has been under regulatory evaluation rather than listed as an approved sunscreen active [1].

Published literature on amiloxate itself consists mainly of analytical methods, environmental occurrence studies, and photoallergy reports [3][4][5]. It is chemically close to octinoxate, the better-known cinnamate UVB filter [1].
infobox: Under evaluation (not an approved OTC active)

paras: Amiloxate is the 3-methylbutyl ester of 4-methoxycinnamic acid, with formula C15H20O3 and a molar mass of about 248 g/mol [1]. Like other organic ('chemical') filters, it is an aromatic molecule that absorbs high-energy ultraviolet light and releases the energy as lower-energy radiation, so less UV reaches the skin [2]. It sits in the UVB filter group alongside other cinnamates such as octinoxate [1][2]. Cinnamates as a class are known to cause allergic contact dermatitis in some people, as filters and as excipients [2].

Amiloxate appears among the UV filters measured in commercial suncare formulations and cosmetics by chromatography methods [3][6][7]. In a mouse inflammation assay of the 21 UV filters then authorised in Europe, 13 showed anti-inflammatory effects; researchers proposed this might explain differences between in vivo and in vitro SPF measurements [8].

The EU approved amiloxate in 1997 under its cosmetics framework, where sunscreen is treated as a cosmetic [1][2]. In the US sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, which makes approval of newer ingredients slower and narrows the ingredient list; amiloxate has been described as undergoing regulatory evaluation there [1][2]. In 2021 the FDA sorted filters into categories, and as of that year only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were listed as generally recognised as safe and effective [2].

A 15-year review of sunscreen allergy found that 20% of 402 patients tested had allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis to one or more UV absorbers [9]. A case report described photoallergic contact dermatitis due to isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate in a sunscreen marketed as organic [4], and another study reported photoallergy to UV filters across several sunscreens [10].

Amiloxate has been measured in indoor dust [11] and in a freshwater recreational reservoir, where researchers examined its dissipation [5]. Porcine-skin work found chemical UV absorbers largely remained in the outer stratum corneum in a barrier-mimetic formulation [12].

No clinical trials specific to amiloxate were found. It was among the filters evaluated in a registered multicentre European photopatch study (1,000 participants) [13], and in the allergy series described above [9].

Amiloxate has little visibility in skincare communities, where discussion of UV filters centres on better-known ones such as octinoxate, oxybenzone, avobenzone and mineral filters. Public-health bodies generally hold that skin cancer risk from sun exposure outweighs the unproven concerns about approved filters, per Wikipedia's sunscreen article [2].

timeline.event: The FDA's administrative order sorted sunscreen filters into three categories [2].
